item.title: An Agent Skill Can Travel. Its Results Still Need Checking.
item.description: Anthropic has donated the Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation. The useful distinction is between sharing a procedure and proving that another agent can carry it out.
item.dc:creator: Tugrul Guner
item.content:encoded:
An AI agent can read documents, use software tools and carry out a task. Knowing how to do the task in general leaves another problem: knowing how a particular team does it. Which records count as evidence? What requires approval? What does a finished result look like?

Agent Skills puts that procedural knowledge in a folder an agent can read. The folder contains instructions and can include supporting references, scripts and templates. A common format lets people share the procedure across agent applications that support the format instead of explaining it again in every conversation.

On October 22, Anthropic announced that it was donating the Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation, a project home under the Linux Foundation. The format was already open. The new development concerns who maintains and guides it as more products depend on the same way of packaging instructions.

That makes a useful distinction visible: a team can carry its procedure to another agent while still having to check whether that agent can perform it.

What travels inside the folder

Consider an illustrative task: reviewing a supplier’s invoice before payment. An agent may be able to read the document, but the team’s process could require matching it to a purchase order, checking whether the goods arrived and referring discrepancies to a person.

A skill can preserve that sequence, the exceptions and the expected report. Its central file, named SKILL.md, starts with a name and description, followed by instructions written as ordinary text. Optional files can hold the detailed policy, a report template or a script used during the task.

This arrangement separates a reusable procedure from the conversation in which someone first explained it. If the team discovers a recurring mistake, it can edit the procedure and share the revised folder. The invoice example here illustrates the format; it is not a tested payment workflow or a reported customer deployment.

The receiving agent still needs the purchase order, delivery record and appropriate tools. A folder explaining how to check those records does not supply access to them. The foundation’s own announcement makes the same boundary explicit: a common format provides shared guidance, while the agent still needs the access and capabilities required for the task.

The agent reads the instructions when they become relevant

Keeping many procedures available creates another problem. Loading every detailed policy into every conversation would make the agent process material unrelated to the current job.

The Agent Skills specification describes staged loading. At the start, the agent receives the names and descriptions of available skills. When a task calls for one, it loads that skill’s full instructions. Supporting files are read when needed. The specification calls this progressive disclosure.

For the invoice review, the short description helps the agent identify the relevant procedure. Loading SKILL.md supplies the sequence to follow. A reference to the purchasing policy then gives it a reason to open that particular supporting file. A different task can use a different procedure without loading the invoice policy at the outset.

Conceptual illustration of the documented loading pattern, using the hypothetical invoice review. It is not a trace from a running agent.

This is a way to organize what enters the model’s working context, meaning the material it can use during the conversation. It does not retrain the model. The instructions are supplied to it as part of doing the task.

The description therefore has an important job. The specification asks authors to explain both what a skill does and when it should be used. A detailed procedure can be present on disk yet fail to help if the agent never identifies it as relevant.

A shared file format leaves implementation choices

Compatibility has several layers. The format specifies the contents of a skill folder. The software running the agent decides how to discover those folders and deliver their contents to the model.

The official integration guide describes agents that read skill files directly and agents that receive them through a dedicated activation tool. It also explains that the specification does not mandate an installation directory. A folder on one laptop is not automatically visible to an agent running on a remote server.

Some details explicitly vary between implementations. The specification marks the optional allowed-tools field, which lists pre-approved tools, as experimental and says support may differ. It also notes that supported scripting languages depend on the agent implementation.

For the invoice procedure, these differences matter at the point of action. The instructions may ask the agent to run a checking script or query a record system. Whether it can do so depends on the receiving environment. Reading the same instructions does not establish identical execution.

Trust is another separate decision. A skill introduces instructions, and it may include executable code. The integration guide recommends considering a trust check before loading skills supplied by an unfamiliar repository, so that a newly downloaded project cannot silently introduce instructions into the agent’s context. A shared format makes those materials easier to distribute; it does not certify that they deserve access.

What the foundation receives

Anthropic says the donation includes the Agent Skills name and logo, its GitHub organization and the agentskills.io domain. The company says people can continue using or contributing to the standard without joining the foundation.

The foundation describes governance through a multi-company Technical Steering Committee. Anthropic names David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as lead maintainers and says engineers from several companies will maintain the standard as individuals.

Versioned releases, a formal proposal process and security guidance appear in Anthropic’s proposed roadmap. Those are proposals in the announcement, rather than completed protections delivered by the donation.

The practical stake is continuity: a team’s accumulated guidance can remain useful when it changes agent applications.

In the invoice example, the same questions still determine success: did the agent inspect the right records, identify the discrepancy and leave payment unchanged when approval was missing? The procedure can travel with those requirements intact. Evidence that the new agent met them has to come from what it actually did.

Sources and further reading

  • Anthropic’s October 22 Agent Skills donation announcement

  • Agentic AI Foundation: sharing team expertise across agents

  • Agent Skills format specification

  • Official guide to adding skills support

item.title: Rounding Can Change What an AI Learns
item.description: How rounding can distort learning signals—and why rearranging the arithmetic can help.
item.dc:creator: Tugrul Guner
item.content:encoded:
An AI model learns by comparing its predictions with training examples and calculating how its internal settings should change. The signals guiding those changes depend on arithmetic performed with a limited number of digits. A new paper examines what happens when rounding removes part of a learning signal, or produces a signal where none should exist. In small training experiments, the difference changed whether learning continued smoothly or was disrupted by sudden jumps.

Jonathan T. Barron, Dan Gnanapragasam and Michael Tschannen of Google DeepMind describe the problem in A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy, posted on October 22. The paper is a preprint, a research manuscript whose results have not been established here as peer-reviewed findings. Its central numerical examples are small enough to inspect directly: two calculations that are equivalent on paper can give a computer different instructions for learning.

How a prediction becomes a correction

Consider a model choosing between three possible labels for an image. This is an illustration of the calculation, rather than an image-recognition experiment from the paper.

The model first assigns each label a score. A larger score means a stronger preference. A function called softmax converts those scores into probabilities that add up to one. A training loss called cross-entropy then measures how poorly those probabilities match the correct label.

The loss also supplies a way to improve the prediction. Its gradient tells the training algorithm how the loss changes when a score changes. The network uses these score-level signals to calculate how the loss depends on its internal settings, often called weights. A separate update algorithm uses that information to change the settings. A score gradient and a change to a weight are different stages of learning.

For this calculation, the correct label receives a gradient equal to its predicted probability minus one. The other labels receive gradients equal to their predicted probabilities. The negative contribution for the correct label and the positive contributions for the alternatives should cancel.

As the model becomes increasingly confident in a correct answer, all these contributions become small. There is less left to correct, but the remaining contributions should retain their relationship.

The problem appears when one part becomes zero before the others do.

A tiny number can survive alone and disappear beside one

Computers commonly represent real numbers using floating-point formats, which store a limited number of significant digits. A small value can be represented on its own while being too small to change a much larger value when the two are added.

The paper’s high-confidence example encounters exactly that situation. After the scores have been rearranged to avoid excessively large numbers, softmax needs to divide by one plus a tiny positive quantity.

That tiny quantity represents the remaining alternatives. If adding it to one rounds the answer back to exactly one, the computed probability for the correct label can become exactly one too. Subtracting one then produces a gradient of zero.

The alternative labels take a different numerical route. Their probabilities are calculated from small values directly, so their gradients can remain positive.

The computer has erased the contribution for the correct answer while retaining the contributions for its alternatives. The gradients no longer cancel as the mathematics requires. Barron and his colleagues call this Softmax Collapse.

Their example uses three scores: 9, −9 and −9, with the first label correct. A local CPU check of the paper’s supplied JAX functions reproduced the problem in 32-bit floating-point arithmetic. The standard cross-entropy returned a loss of zero and a correct-label gradient of zero. Each alternative still had a gradient of approximately 0.0000000152.

Those values are tiny. Their unequal disappearance is what matters.

The fix preserves the small quantity

The authors change the route through the calculation while preserving the intended mathematical objective.

Instead of obtaining the tiny correct-label gradient by subtracting one from a probability almost equal to one, the reformulation preserves the small quantity directly. It calculates the correct-label gradient as the negative sum of the contributions for the alternatives.

The loss calculation also uses a numerically stable function that can retain a small result even when forming “one plus a tiny quantity” first would have rounded away the information.

For the same three scores, the corrected function returned a loss of approximately 0.0000000305. The correct-label gradient was approximately −0.0000000305, balancing the two positive contributions from the alternatives.

Local CPU reproduction of the paper’s three-score example in 32-bit arithmetic. Values are rounded for display. These are gradients with respect to prediction scores, not measurements of model-training accuracy.

A separate calculation using 100-digit arithmetic confirmed the expected loss and gradients to the precision relevant to these displayed values. This checks the numerical example, not the paper’s complete training experiments.

The improvement comes from how the arithmetic is organized. More digits can postpone the original failure, but they do not remove the underlying cancellation problem.

Why a small error can disrupt training

A small gradient does not necessarily produce a proportionally small training step. Adam, an algorithm used to update a model’s internal settings, adjusts the scale of its steps using the recent history of gradients.

The paper connects this adaptation to a previously reported pattern called the Slingshot phenomenon. After a model has learned its training examples, the measured loss can remain near zero and then suddenly spike.

In the authors’ account, highly confident predictions cross the rounding threshold and lose their correct-label gradients. The resulting gradients for the model’s weights become very small, and Adam’s running estimate of their squared magnitude decays. Later changes to the weights can bring examples back across the threshold, abruptly restoring the missing score-level contributions. These feed into the gradients for the weights. Adam divides its averaged weight gradients by a scale based on the square root of that decaying estimate, plus a small stabilizing constant. The return of the gradients can therefore produce a large change to the weights.

The authors tested this mechanism on small networks learning arithmetic with remainders. Such tasks are used to study grokking: a model first memorizes training examples and only later begins answering unseen examples correctly.

In one reported test, networks had to square two numbers, add them, and return the remainder after division by 97. Without weight decay, the penalty that shrinks the model’s weights, a loss spike dropped test accuracy from 61% to 23%. With the corrected cross-entropy, the comparison run continued smoothly to 85%. The paper also reports removing the spikes in other arithmetic tasks and numerical formats.

These are the authors’ training results, not results reproduced for this article. The paper explicitly notes that the extreme confidence levels and near-identical model outputs it studies are uncommon in standard large-scale training. Its experiments do not establish an accuracy improvement for every model trained with cross-entropy, or explain every sudden change in learning.

What they show is more specific: in these settings, a numerical artifact inside the loss calculation can change the training trajectory.

A model can also receive a correction after it already matches

The second problem appears when one model learns to match another model’s predictions, a process called distillation. The teacher supplies a distribution of probabilities, and the student is trained to reproduce it.

If their scores are identical, the student already matches the teacher. The gradient with respect to the student’s scores should be zero.

Standard calculations can nevertheless produce a small residual. The teacher’s probabilities and the quantities used to calculate the student’s gradient are obtained through slightly different sequences of operations. Rounding can leave a discrepancy even when both begin with identical scores.

Here the arithmetic creates a signal that should be absent. Barron and his colleagues call this Softmax Cancellation. Their fix starts with the difference between the student’s and teacher’s scores and uses functions designed to preserve small differences.

In the local check, identical teacher and student scores produced small nonzero gradients with the standard calculation. The corrected function returned zeros. For a second example with slightly different scores, its gradients also agreed closely with an independently computed 100-digit reference.

The paper carries the idea into a deliberately revealing training experiment: the student begins as an exact copy of the teacher. The authors report that ordinary calculations can still move it away, especially in a lower-precision format. Their corrected loss kept it matched in the tested settings.

The two examples show how finite-precision arithmetic can alter the signals that a training objective is meant to provide. Preserving those signals can change whether a model continues correcting a real difference or starts responding to one created by the calculation itself.

Sources and further reading

  • A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy, arXiv version 1

  • Authors’ project page and interactive demonstration

item.title: What Is Space Made Of?
item.description: Physicists changed nothing but quantum information and the space itself changed shape. If that sounds backwards, it may be because we’ve been thinking about what space is the wrong way around.
item.dc:creator: Tugrul Guner
item.content:encoded:
What is space made of? Physics can describe what occupies space, how long light takes to cross it and how it bends around anything heavy. It has no settled answer for what space itself consists of.

The question becomes unavoidable at the beginning of the universe.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

TLDR. Nobody knows what space itself is made of. One idea says it is not a basic ingredient of the universe at all, but something built out of the links between very small quantum things. Temperature works the same way: no single molecule has one, but a whole crowd of them does. You cannot test that on real space, so physicists build toy versions of space instead. A toy is a few quantum particles, linked to each other so that the pattern of links behaves the way a small patch of space behaves. Because it behaves like space, it has a size you can measure. Toys like this have existed since 2015, and every one of them had the same flaw. Put something heavy into real space and the space around it bends. Bending means its distances and areas actually change, and that change is what gravity is. So a toy behaving like space should do the same: put something inside it and its size should change. None of them did. The size stayed exactly what it had been before, as though nothing had been put in at all. In 2025 a proof identified what had been missing: a quantum property called magic. In July 2026 a team added magic to one of these toys and ran it on a quantum computer, a machine built to hold links like these. They put something inside, and this time the size changed. Two things here are strange. The first is where the space actually is. Picture a room with writing covering its walls, and the writing describes the room: how big it is, how far across, what is sitting on the floor in the middle. Now take the room away and keep only the walls. In these toys, that is all there is. The particles are the writing. The space is what the writing describes. And that ought to be impossible. A wall is flat and a room is not, so work out how much you would have to write down to pin every point inside, and you run out of wall long before you finish. Black holes were the first hint that the arithmetic is wrong. The second is bigger. We treat information as a record of the world: measurements, descriptions, facts about things that already exist. In this picture the order is reversed. Change the links between the particles and the space itself changes. One arrangement of links gives you a stretch of space of a certain size. Another splits it into two pieces with no route between them. Nothing is moved and nothing is built. Only the information changes, and the space changes with it.

Run the best model we have backwards far enough, past the galaxies and the first atoms, and everything we can now see ends up squeezed into a space smaller than a single atom. General relativity describes gravity by calculating how matter changes space and time. Quantum physics predicts the behaviour of atoms and particles using probabilities. For stars and planets, quantum effects are usually too small to affect the calculation. For atoms and particles, gravity is usually too weak to affect the calculation. The early universe was both extremely small and extremely dense, so neither description could be ignored. Physics still has no experimentally established theory that combines them under those conditions.

A familiar fact about temperature suggests a possible way forward. A single molecule can move quickly or slowly, but one molecule does not have a temperature of its own. Temperature appears only when many molecules are considered together. Physicists call this emergence: a property of the whole arises from the behaviour of many smaller parts.

One line of research asks whether space could form in a similar way. Individual quantum objects may not carry distance or area by themselves. Those features may arise only from patterns in how many quantum objects behave and relate to each other. Physicists use quantum information to describe those possible behaviours and relationships. Space would then work like temperature: not something each part carries, but something the pattern has.

How the boundary can describe the inside

One approach to this idea is called holography. It asks whether quantum information describing the inside of a region can be encoded around its outer boundary. That raises a practical question. How can information about the inside be spread around the edge and still be recovered?

The HaPPY model offered a mathematical example in 2015. It represented quantum information with qubits, the basic information units of a quantum computer. Instead of placing the complete interior description in one boundary qubit, HaPPY encoded it as a pattern shared across many. Suitable groups of boundary qubits could recover the original information even when some were unavailable. This method is called quantum error correction, making HaPPY a quantum error-correcting code.

Imagine a circular room with a chair at its centre. A written record describes the chair and includes the line “Chair position: centre.” The record has been divided into pieces and stored in boxes around the wall. One box gives you only part of the record. Open enough of the right boxes and you can reconstruct the complete description.

The room makes the quantum process visible. The area inside the room represents the model’s interior. The wall represents its boundary. The chair record represents quantum information assigned to the interior. The pieces in the boxes represent the encoded pattern shared among boundary qubits. Opening enough boxes represents recovering the interior information from part of the boundary.

Recovering the interior information was HaPPY’s central achievement. Gravity adds another requirement. Matter affects geometry, so a change in the description of matter should produce a change in the description of geometry.

Two things about this room can be written down: where the chair is, and what the geometry is, meaning the distances and areas of the space around it. Now move the chair from the centre toward the wall. The first record has to be rewritten, because the matter is in a new place. A model of gravity has to rewrite the second one as well, because the distribution of matter has changed. An ordinary chair would alter spacetime by an immeasurably small amount, but the sequence is what matters here: move the matter, then update the geometry associated with it.

Original HaPPY managed the first and not the second. It could accept the chair’s new position and rewrite that record. Its geometry had been fixed when the model was built. The chair moved; the distances and areas still described the old arrangement. That is what physicists mean when they call HaPPY’s geometry fixed.

This was the limitation the July 2026 experiment set out to address. Could a modified HaPPY model let geometry respond to matter without losing its ability to recover the interior from the boundary? Two pieces have to come first: why geometry must respond at all, and which quantum relationship might allow it to.

Why gravity requires geometry to respond

The importance of a responsive geometry comes from Einstein’s account of gravity. Einstein treated space and time as one physical structure called spacetime. Its geometry determines distances, areas and elapsed time. Matter and energy change that geometry, and the changed geometry determines how matter moves.

The Sun’s mass changes the spacetime around it. Earth’s orbit is the path Earth follows through that changed spacetime. Earth also changes spacetime around itself. Because time is part of spacetime, Earth’s mass changes the rate at which clocks run at different heights.

That change is measurable across less than the height of a person. In 2010, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology compared two atomic clocks placed just 33 centimetres apart in height, roughly the length of a school ruler. An atomic clock counts extremely regular changes inside atoms. The lower clock counted slightly fewer changes than the higher one. Slightly less time had passed for it.

Einstein’s equations predict these effects. What they do not do is say what spacetime consists of at its smallest scale. Quantum physics describes matter at the scale of atoms and smaller particles, and no experimentally established account connects that description of matter with spacetime itself. Einstein tells you what geometry does. Nobody can yet tell you what it is.

Geometry from quantum information

Holography gave quantum information a possible role: information on a boundary could describe an interior. HaPPY showed how parts of that boundary could recover the interior description. Its fixed geometry exposed what was still missing. Recovering a description of the inside does not explain how its distances and areas arise, or how they change when matter changes.

The temperature comparison suggested where distance and area might come from: relationships among many quantum objects. Any account built from those relationships must also reproduce the behaviour already established by general relativity. When matter changes, geometry changes with it. Researchers pursuing this idea therefore needed a quantum relationship that could account for interior geometry while allowing that geometry to respond to a changed matter state. Entanglement became the leading candidate.

How entanglement works

Two quantum objects, such as photons or atoms, can become entangled when they are created together or made to interact. Afterward, predictions about their measurement results require one shared description of the pair. Describing either object by itself leaves out part of the information. Researchers can move the objects apart while preserving this relationship long enough to test it.

This produces a measurable effect. Send the objects to separate laboratories and let each laboratory choose independently how to measure its object. An individual result can look random. Compare the results from many pairs, however, and a pattern appears between them.

Imagine two contestants placed in separate rooms. They cannot communicate, and each receives one of several questions chosen at random. Before they are separated, they may agree on a list of answers for every possible question. John Bell showed that any such prearranged strategy places a limit on the pattern of matching and differing answers they can produce. Experiments with entangled quantum objects exceed that limit. No separate answer list carried by each object can reproduce the measured pattern. Each laboratory still sees unpredictable results, so the relationship cannot be used to send a message. It appears only when the two sets of results are later compared.

In holographic models, entanglement connects to geometry in two ways. It determines the area of a surface inside, and it determines whether two regions of the interior remain joined at all. Both appear below in a form you can picture. The question they raise comes first.

Why should entanglement at the boundary reveal an area inside? The first clue came from black holes.

Black holes connect area and information

A black hole has a boundary called a horizon. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that a black hole has entropy. Imagine a theatre where every seat is occupied. People can exchange seats in many ways while the sign outside still reports the same fact: full. Entropy counts how many hidden arrangements fit the unchanged description seen from outside.

For ordinary matter, the number of possible arrangements usually grows with volume. A larger container can hold more particles in more configurations. Black-hole entropy follows a different rule: it grows with the area of the horizon.

The relationship does not say what those microscopic arrangements are. It says a surface can count them. That was enough to start a field.

Gravity inside, quantum physics on the boundary

The guess that turned the clue into a program came in the early 1990s, from Gerard ‘t Hooft and Leonard Susskind. If a black hole’s surface can count everything inside it, perhaps that is not a peculiarity of black holes. Perhaps it is a rule about space itself: take any region, and everything inside it can be recorded on its boundary. They named it the holographic principle, after holograms, the flat images that hold a whole three-dimensional scene. It was a principle without a working example. Nobody could write down a single case where it demonstrably held.

In 1997, Juan Maldacena proposed a specific and influential version of holography. In the special spacetime he studied, a quantum theory with no gravity on the boundary and a theory of gravity in the interior could describe the same physics.

Picture an orange before it is cut. Its peel represents the boundary, and the fruit beneath it represents the interior. You can move across the peel while remaining on its surface. To enter the fruit, you need another direction: inward, away from the peel and toward the centre. The interior therefore has one more spatial direction than the boundary. Maldacena’s idea says that a quantum theory living on the boundary can still contain everything needed to describe the interior, including this extra direction and its geometry.

The proposed equivalence is mathematical, it has never been proved, and it applies to a special type of spacetime. The boundary is not a physical wall around the observable universe, and Maldacena’s spacetime differs from the universe astronomers observe.

In 2006, Shinsei Ryu and Tadashi Takayanagi found a formula linking entanglement at the boundary to the area of a surface inside. Return to the orange and draw a line around its middle. The peel above the line is the chosen boundary section. The peel below it is the rest of the boundary. Now imagine cutting the orange along that line. The cut exposes a circular face between the two halves. The fruit is still the interior, and the circular face lies between its upper and lower halves. The Ryu–Takayanagi formula uses the entanglement between the quantum information on the upper and lower parts of the peel to calculate the area of this cross-section. It does not calculate the total volume of the fruit. The important result was that entanglement between two parts of the boundary could reveal one property of the interior: the area of the circular cross-section between its upper and lower halves.

Mark Van Raamsdonk asked in 2010 whether entanglement prevents the interior from splitting into separate spaces. Return to an uncut orange. The fruit runs continuously from the top of the orange to the bottom, with no empty gap breaking it into separate pieces. This represents a connected interior. As the entanglement between the upper and lower parts of the peel decreases, imagine the fruit becoming narrower around the middle. If the entanglement is reduced far enough, the narrow middle disappears. A gap then separates the fruit at the top from the fruit at the bottom. In the model, this represents two interior regions with no path connecting them.

These results apply within a special family of holographic theories. They do not establish that the space around us is made of entanglement. What they establish is narrower and still worth having: inside those theories, entanglement decides an area, and it decides whether there is one interior or two.

How HaPPY linked entanglement to area

The problem was still HaPPY’s fixed geometry. HaPPY could recover interior information from the boundary, but changing its matter-like information left the geometry unchanged. The orange showed a possible way forward: entanglement between two parts of the peel determined the area of the circular face inside the fruit. If the entanglement changed, the calculated area could change too. Researchers therefore asked whether HaPPY could use this relationship to let its interior area respond instead of remaining fixed. The obstacle lay in the way the original HaPPY model was built.

The original HaPPY model was created in 2015 by Fernando Pastawski, Beni Yoshida, Daniel Harlow and John Preskill. Letters from their surnames form its name. Return to the room and the chair record. The boxes around the wall represent the boundary units that eventually hold the encoded pieces of the record. To show how those pieces reach the wall, add relay boxes in the space between the chair and the boundary boxes. Each relay box receives encoded information, repackages it and passes pieces to relay boxes farther outward. One direct transfer from one box to the next is a handoff. In the actual HaPPY code, the relay boxes represent encoding operations and the handoffs represent fixed quantum connections between them.

Now divide the boundary boxes into two groups. Label the boxes along one half of the circular wall A and the boxes along the other half B. The aim is to find how much entanglement links these boundary groups. To continue the division through the interior of the room, temporarily label every relay box A or B as well. The labels do not alter the boxes or create new handoffs. They only decide which side of this imagined division contains each relay box.

Follow one existing handoff between two relay boxes. Call them Relay Box 1 and Relay Box 2. If both boxes have been labelled A, the transfer begins and ends inside group A, so it is not counted. If both have been labelled B, it remains inside group B and is not counted. Now label Relay Box 1 as A and Relay Box 2 as B. The same handoff now begins at a box assigned to group A and arrives at a box assigned to group B. Count it, because this fixed quantum connection directly links the two groups. No box crosses the division. The handoff is counted solely because the two boxes it connects were assigned to different groups.

There are many possible ways to label the relay boxes. Each choice produces a different boundary between A and B and may leave a different number of handoffs connecting the groups. HaPPY compares these choices and keeps the smallest count. Each counted handoff carries the same amount of entanglement, so in this code the smallest count gives the entanglement that the wiring itself creates between the two boundary groups. Anything stored inside can carry entanglement of its own, and that share adds on top of the count.

Return to the orange used earlier to picture the relationship between boundary entanglement and interior area. The peel represented the boundary, and the fruit represented the interior. The peel was divided into upper and lower sections. An imagined cut through the fruit exposed a circular face between them. The Ryu–Takayanagi rule said that the entanglement between the two peel sections corresponded to the area of that circular face.

One detail of the Ryu–Takayanagi rule matters here. The upper and lower sections of peel meet along a ring around the orange. Imagine two ways to divide the fruit while keeping that ring fixed. One cut travels straight across the middle and produces the flat circular face we have already pictured. Another cut begins at the same ring, curves upward through the fruit and returns to the ring all the way around, producing a bowl-shaped face. Both faces meet the peel along the same ring and separate the same upper and lower sections, but the curved face has a larger area. The rule therefore uses the flat circular face, which has the smallest area.

HaPPY reproduced this choice with whole-number counting. Group A corresponds to the upper section of the peel and group B to the lower section. Each way of labelling the relay boxes A or B creates one possible division through the model’s interior. For each division, HaPPY counts the existing handoffs that directly connect an A-labelled relay box to a B-labelled relay box. Every such handoff adds one to the total and represents the same fixed amount of entanglement. Different divisions can produce different totals, so HaPPY keeps the smallest one. That smallest handoff count is the code’s version of selecting the interior surface with the smallest area. It represents the area of the orange’s flat circular face.

This was also the limitation. HaPPY’s handoffs were fixed when the code was built. Changing the matter-like information in the interior did not add, remove or rearrange them. Repeating the search through all possible divisions therefore returned the same smallest count, and the same area for the circular face. Einstein’s theory requires geometry to change when matter and energy change. HaPPY’s could not. The missing response has a name, back-reaction, and it is what the July experiment went after.

The quantum-computer experiment

Original HaPPY always returned the same smallest handoff count because its quantum connections were fixed. Debopriyo Biswas, Gong Cheng, Krishnanand Karthikeyan and twelve colleagues asked whether selected boundary qubits could continue to reconstruct the original interior input while an area-like quantity changed with the matter-like information inside the code.

The team ran a reduced HaPPY-like code on IonQ Forte, a quantum computer that performs calculations by controlling electrically charged atoms. The full construction would have required 25 qubits, but the researchers reduced the part needed for this test to eight qubits while preserving the information quantities they wanted to measure.

Here is how the room example maps onto the machine. At the start of each run, two of the eight hardware qubits held the quantum input. They played the part of the chair record: they held the information before it was distributed. The other six qubits began in a fixed blank state so they could take part in the encoding.

Why begin with two input qubits? The first carried the information that the code would spread across the boundary and later rebuild. The second gave the researchers another qubit with which to entangle the first. At first, the pair shared no entanglement. The researchers then entangled them a little, then more. As that link grew, the first qubit could no longer be fully described on its own; part of its description now depended on the pair. Physicists express this change by saying that the first qubit’s entropy increased. The experiment treated that entropy as the model’s matter contribution. Each new entanglement setting changed only how the two input qubits were prepared before encoding. For each version of the code, the researchers sent every newly prepared pair through the same encoding circuit. In this way, they changed the matter contribution while leaving the circuit’s arrangement untouched.

The circuit then performed a sequence of operations on those same eight qubits. It did not create new qubits or remove the two that held the input. Instead, it mixed the input with the six blank qubits. After this encoding, the original division between two input qubits and six helpers no longer applied. All eight now carried parts of the encoded information, so all eight served as the code’s boundary qubits. The researchers later selected three of these eight boundary qubits and tested whether those three could reconstruct the original state of the first input qubit.

Why did the researchers reconstruct only the first input qubit? The selected three boundary qubits corresponded to a particular portion of the model’s interior. The first input belonged to that portion; the second did not. Although both inputs had been encoded across all eight boundary qubits, this selected group of three could rebuild the first input’s state but not the second’s.

The second input still affected the test. Its entanglement with the first made the first input’s entropy rise. The researchers could therefore use the second input to change the entropy inside the selected interior portion without placing the second input itself inside that portion.

The holographic relationship being tested predicted how this should appear at the boundary. It said that the entropy of the selected three-qubit boundary section should equal the entropy of the first input qubit plus an area contribution. The researchers could measure the boundary entropy, subtract the first input qubit’s entropy and see whether the area-like remainder stayed fixed or changed. No physical matter was added or moved.

Why entanglement was not enough

The holographic relationship separates the boundary entropy into two parts. One is associated with interior area. The other is the entropy of the quantum information inside the selected interior region. In a physical theory, that information could be carried by particles and fields. This small code contained no particles or fields, so the entropy of the first input qubit filled that place in the calculation. Entangling the first input with the second raised the first input’s entropy. That is how the researchers increased the code’s stand-in for the matter contribution. Original HaPPY still gave the same area every time, because the operations that encoded those inputs followed a fixed pattern. The team therefore needed to change something about the encoding itself.

The change involved a quantum property called magic. Despite its name, magic describes a practical dividing line in quantum computing. Imagine shuffling a deck with a limited set of moves. Those moves may produce complicated arrangements, yet a short rule can still track where every card must be. Original HaPPY’s operations belong to a similarly trackable family.

Other quantum operations break that convenient pattern. Tracking the resulting state requires more than the shortcut. Quantum-information researchers call this extra computational resource magic. It is separate from entanglement. Entanglement says that several qubits share a description. Magic says that their complete arrangement has escaped the restricted family that the shortcut can track.

Magic also breaks the counting rule from earlier. That rule worked because every handoff carried the same fixed amount of entanglement: count the crossed handoffs and you had the total. Once the operations leave the trackable family, that is no longer true. How much entanglement a connection carries now depends on what was encoded, so the total is no longer settled by the wiring alone.

Researchers had a reason to suspect that this distinction mattered for geometry. In 2025, in the peer-reviewed journal PRX Quantum, ChunJun Cao, Gong Cheng and four colleagues proved a sharp version of it for a class of holographic theories: “the non-local magic vanishes if and only if there is no gravitational back-reaction.” No magic, no response. A proposal released in March 2026 then described a HaPPY-like code whose area term could respond to the interior state once magic entered the encoding.

The July team brought a reduced version of that proposal to the IonQ processor. They made small changes to the angles of selected operations in the encoding circuit. One version kept original HaPPY’s shortcut-friendly operations. Other versions contained increasing amounts of magic. The team passed the same series of two-qubit input states through each version, allowing a direct comparison.

Watching the area-like remainder move

For every input state and every version of the encoding, the team repeated measurements in several ways. Combining those results allowed them to reconstruct the state of the selected three-qubit boundary section and the original state of the first input qubit. This process is called quantum state tomography.

The researchers then calculated the entropy of each reconstructed state. One number described the selected boundary section. The other described the first input qubit that those three boundary qubits could rebuild. The holographic relationship predicted that subtracting the second number from the first would leave the area contribution:

entropy of the selected boundary section
- entropy of the reconstructed first input qubit
= proto-area entropy

The logic resembles weighing a packed suitcase, subtracting the weight of its contents and assigning the remainder to the suitcase. Here, the two quantities were entropies rather than weights. The remainder occupied the place assigned to area in the holographic relationship, so the researchers called it proto-area entropy. It was an information quantity calculated from repeated measurements. It did not describe a physical surface inside the processor.

Original HaPPY behaved as expected. Increasing the entanglement between the two input qubits raised the boundary entropy. It also raised the entropy of the first input qubit by almost the same amount. Once the researchers subtracted one increase from the other, the proto-area remained nearly unchanged.

The magic-containing versions broke that lockstep. As the input entanglement increased, the boundary entropy and the first input qubit’s entropy changed by different amounts. Their difference grew. Adding more magic made the response stronger.

That difference is the whole result. The matter contribution changed. The three selected boundary qubits still rebuilt an approximation of the first input state. And this time the area-like remainder moved with it, which is the one thing the original code could never do.

There is an important qualification. The magic-containing code reconstructed the first input state only approximately. To keep the experiment manageable on current hardware, the team used a shorter, restricted reconstruction circuit. Their calculations showed that this restriction made the proto-area response look larger. A more flexible numerical reconstruction still found a changing proto-area, though the change was smaller. The response survived the better reconstruction, while its reported size depended partly on the method used to extract the first input state.

What this does not establish

More is missing here than is present, and it is worth being plain about which is which.

The 2025 theorem has been through peer review. The March 2026 proposal and the July 2026 experiment have not. They are preprints, and published versions can change. Cao and Cheng are authors on all three, so this is one research line checking its own work rather than separate groups arriving at the same place. A trapped-ion group in Innsbruck has run related holographic codes on its own hardware, but nobody has reproduced the proto-area response.

The model is also a toy, and a small one. It lives in Maldacena’s special spacetime rather than ours. It contains no time: nothing moves and nothing happens in it, and the origin of the universe is a question about time. The proto-area is an information quantity, not a surface anyone measured inside the processor. Eight qubits are eight qubits.

Asked in June how close this line of work comes to a theory of gravity, Cao told Quanta Magazine: “You satisfy one of the necessary conditions. Right now, we are at step 0.5 of 5.”

Why this matters to me

I do not work in this field, and everything below is a reader’s reaction rather than a contribution. The sections above are what the papers report.

What space is made of is one of the oldest questions we have, and every answer physics ever tried was made of stuff: particles, strings, some finer grain of matter. The candidate here is not stuff. It is information, and what pulls me in hardest is what kind of information it turns out to be. There are two ways to describe a collection of things. One lists each thing’s own properties: this car’s engine, its speed, its position. The other ignores the things themselves and describes what runs between them: which car is bound for which destination, how the routes cross, what is paired with what. The first kind of information sits inside the objects. The second kind sits in no object at all. Inspect one car as closely as you like, engine, paint, wheels, and nothing on it tells you which destination it is bound for or which other car it is paired with. That fact is not stored in the car, and not in the destination either. It lives only in the two of them together. Entanglement is the second kind taken to its extreme: a pair of particles can be arranged so that each one, alone, says nothing, and everything there is to know is written in the relation.

And the claim of this whole line of research is that space is built from the second kind. The particles on the boundary do not matter one by one. What matters is the web of relations running among them. Count the relations crossing between two halves of the web and you have an area inside. Thin them out and the interior narrows; cut them and it falls into two. A direction that does not exist on the surface, the inward one, is woven entirely out of how the pieces are coupled. In these models, volume is what a web of relationships looks like from the inside.

Then comes the part I cannot get over. The boundary is flat, and the rules running on it contain no gravity at all: quantum particles, linked and interacting on a surface, nothing more. Read that same pattern as a volume, and gravity is there. Nothing was added in between. The same physics, written one way, has no gravity in it; written the other way, it does. This is why the hologram is the right comparison, and it is stronger than it sounds. The depth in a hologram is not stored on the film, but it is not fake either: it is what the flat pattern becomes when you look at it as a scene. In these models gravity is like that. Nothing extra is poured into the volume. Gravity is what the entanglement on the boundary looks like once the pattern is read as space: a fabric woven out of information, and woven so well that it bends, carries planets, and holds you in your chair.

If that is really how it works, then two of the deepest puzzles in physics may be one puzzle seen from two sides. Entanglement is the strangest feature of the quantum world. Gravity is the one force that has refused for a century to be made quantum. In these models they are two readings of the same pattern: entanglement is what it looks like on the boundary, gravity is what it looks like in the volume. And that would carry a lesson about the century of failure. Nobody ever went hunting for the particle of temperature, because temperature is not an ingredient; it is what a crowd of molecules adds up to. If gravity is what entanglement adds up to, then quantizing it like the other forces was never going to work, and the failure itself was a clue. I do not know whether any of this is true. It hints that there is a layer underneath spacetime, and that we may have started reading it.

The other thing I cannot leave alone is what the model is missing. It has no time. Nothing in it moves or happens, and the question that makes quantum gravity worth wanting, what happened at the beginning, is a question about time. But follow this whole line of work one step further. If space is not a basic ingredient, why would time be? And if time also emerges, then asking what came before the Big Bang may be like asking what the pattern was doing before there was a pattern. It would not be a mystery; it would be a question built wrong. It is fascinating where we are heading to. This is why I read these papers at all.

Everything is explainable, those we dont have answer today will have it one day if not today. And I’m looking forward to it!

Sources

Core papers

  • ChunJun Cao, Gong Cheng, Alioscia Hamma, Lorenzo Leone, William Munizzi, Salvatore F. E. Oliviero, “Gravitational back-reaction is magical,” PRX Quantum 6, 040375 (2025). Peer-reviewed. arXiv:2403.07056

  • ChunJun Cao, Gong Cheng, Krishnanand Karthikeyan, Cathy Li, John Preskill, “State-dependent geometries from magic-enriched quantum codes,” arXiv:2603.13475 (13 March 2026). Preprint.

  • Debopriyo Biswas, Gong Cheng, Krishnanand Karthikeyan, Diana Muñoz-Valencia, Vincent P. Su, Hrant Gharibyan, Daiwei Zhu, Grant Salton, Evgeny Epifanovsky, Martin Roetteler, Christopher Monroe, John Preskill, Norbert M. Linke, ChunJun Cao, Crystal Noel, “Observation of gravity-like signatures in holographic codes on a quantum computer,” arXiv:2607.12047 (13 July 2026). Preprint.

  • Alex Steiner, Gerard Anglès Munné, Robert Freund et al., “Holographic quantum codes with trapped ions,” arXiv:2607.16503 (17 July 2026). Preprint; independent implementation of related codes, not a replication of the magic-dependent proto-area result.

Foundations

  • Fernando Pastawski, Beni Yoshida, Daniel Harlow, John Preskill, “Holographic quantum error-correcting codes: Toy models for the bulk/boundary correspondence,” JHEP 06 (2015) 149.

  • Shinsei Ryu, Tadashi Takayanagi, “Holographic Derivation of Entanglement Entropy from AdS/CFT,” Phys. Rev. Lett. 96, 181602 (2006). arXiv:hep-th/0603001

  • Mark Van Raamsdonk, “Building up spacetime with quantum entanglement,” Gen. Rel. Grav. 42, 2323–2329 (2010). arXiv:1005.3035

item.title: When Learning Happens All at Once
item.description: In AI, sudden "grokking" is being formalized as a physics phase transition. In the brain, learning often arrives in abrupt jumps, not only smooth curves. Learning that arrives as a switch, not a slope
item.dc:creator: Tugrul Guner
item.content:encoded:
We picture learning as a curve: steady improvement, a little more each day. Often it isn’t. A system can train for a long time with almost no visible progress, then improve suddenly… The whole capability appearing at once. This happens in artificial neural networks. It happens in the brain. And in the machine case, that abrupt jump is now being written in the exact mathematical language physicists use for phase transitions; the framework that describes water freezing or a magnet aligning.

Several recent papers, published across 2023 and 2026, describe learning as an abrupt transition rather than a smooth climb. Some in artificial networks, some in the brain. What follows is what they found, where the connection is solid, and where it is still an open question. That distinction is the whole point.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

We don’t have one theory of learning

Start with an admission: there is no single, settled account of how learning happens. There are competing pictures, argued over for decades.

The textbook one is gradual. Skill accrues in small increments, the loss curve slides down, practice adds up. It is intuitive, and for some kinds of learning it fits.

The long-standing challenger is that learning is often abrupt. Look at individual learners instead of group averages and acquisition frequently looks step-like, flat, then a jump. Gallistel and colleagues made this case sharply in 2004: the smooth learning curve in the textbooks may be an artifact of averaging, because different individuals jump at different times, and averaging across them smears real discontinuities into a gentle slope.

Both pictures are partly right. The honest position is that abrupt and gradual learning coexist, and which one you see depends on the task, the timescale, the individual, and how you measure. This piece follows the abrupt thread, not because it is the whole story, but because something new is happening there: it is the thread that AI has just tied to physics. The question stops being whether learning can jump, and becomes whether the jump has a describable structure. In machines, the answer is starting to look like yes, and the structure is a phase transition.

What a phase transition actually is

The term does a lot of work in this piece, so it’s worth thirty seconds. A phase transition is one of the most familiar things in nature, even if the name isn’t. Cool water degree by degree and, for a long time, nothing dramatic happens. It just gets colder. Then, at 0°C, it doesn’t get slightly more solid. It becomes ice. The change is sudden, it happens at a precise threshold, and the whole substance reorganizes into a new state at once. Heat a magnet and it loses its magnetism the same way: fine, fine, fine, then gone, all at a single critical temperature.

What makes physicists care is that this isn’t vague. There is exact mathematics for it: a critical point where the transition happens, and an order parameter; some measurable quantity that is essentially zero on one side and suddenly nonzero on the other, marking the switch from one regime to the next. That toolkit was built for water and magnets. The claim running through the new work is that the same toolkit might describe something no one expected: the moment a system learns.

Memorizing isn’t learning

Grokking only sounds strange once you know the difference between two things a neural network can do, so it is worth making explicit. A model can memorize; store its training examples and hand them back perfectly, like a student who has learned last year’s exam answers by heart. Or it can generalize; pull out the underlying rule and apply it to examples it has never seen, like the student who actually understands the method and can solve a fresh problem. Memorizing looks like success on the training set; generalizing is the real thing, and it is what we mean by learning.

Hold on to that distinction, because grokking is what happens when the two come apart in time… The network memorizes first and only much later, suddenly, starts to generalize. That is the jump the rest of this piece is about.

Machines: grokking, and the physics of the jump

The cleanest example is grokking. First documented in 2022, it is one of the strangest behaviors in deep learning: a network trains, quickly memorizes its training data, and then generalizes to nothing… Test performance stays at chance for thousands of steps past the point of overfitting. Then, abruptly, long after it seemed to have stalled, the network generalizes. Test accuracy jumps from near-zero to near-perfect. The capability was not there, and then it was.

For years this was a curiosity. Now it is being described as a phase transition in a literal, not metaphorical, sense.

One 2026 preprint, “Grokking as Dimensional Phase Transition in Neural Networks,” tracks a measurable quantity, the effective dimensionality of the network’s dynamics, across training. It crosses a critical threshold at the moment generalization switches on, moving from one regime to another the way a physical system does at a critical point. The authors report the crossing is robust across network topologies and reflects the geometry of the gradient field, not the specific architecture. The jump has a signature, and the signature is the one physics uses to identify a phase transition.

A second 2026 preprint pushes the physics further. “Learning as a Geometric Phase Transition,” by Le Pera and Nordio, applies the renormalization group and spontaneous symmetry breaking, the two pillars of the modern theory of phase transitions, directly to feature learning. In their account, a symmetric, featureless state becomes unstable during training, and specialized features crystallize out of it, exactly as order emerges when a symmetry breaks in a physical system. Learning, in this framing, is not optimization inching downhill. It is a system passing through a critical point and reorganizing.

Both are preprints, not yet peer-reviewed, and the field is still arguing about mechanism. But the direction is unmistakable: the sudden jumps in machine learning are being explained with the mathematics of phase transitions, and grokking is the sharpest case.

Brains: learning that jumps

The machine story has a biological echo, and it is not about a single flash of insight, but about how brains actually acquire a skill over time. The textbook picture is the smooth learning curve: practice, and performance rises a little each session. Looked at closely, it often doesn’t.

A 2023 study in Nature Communications by Manzur and colleagues, “The behavioral signature of stepwise learning strategy in male rats and its neural correlate in the basal forebrain,” recorded from the basal forebrain while rats learned a task. The rats did not improve gradually. They learned in discrete steps; starting from the behavioral event closest to the reward and then, in jumps, folding in earlier events, and basal-forebrain “bursting” neurons, carrying a reward-prediction-error signal, tracked each step as it emerged. The learning curve was a staircase, not a ramp.

A 2026 study, also in Nature Communications, by Moore and colleagues, “Revealing abrupt transitions from goal-directed to habitual behavior,” is the sharper parallel to grokking. Mice trained until they were expert at a task. Then thousands of trials later, long after performance had plateaued, they flipped from goal-directed control to habit abruptly, within about three trials. The authors call it a “switch-like mechanism”: in the dorsal striatum, outcome-related activity dropped and stimulus-response activity sharpened, rather than drifting over. The behavior looked stable the entire time. The internal reorganization was sudden.

Read that against grokking and the shape is the same: a long stretch where nothing visible changes, then an abrupt internal reorganization that flips the system into a new regime. Systems neuroscientists have begun re-reading their own data this way, a 2022 review, “Slow or sudden: re-interpreting the learning curve for modern systems neuroscience,” argues that learning curves which look gradual may in fact be sudden underneath.

None of this means learning is always a jump. It means abrupt learning is real, replicable, and now visible down to the neurons… Enough to take the thread seriously.

The shared shape, and the honest caveat

Line them up and the common shape is clear: in both artificial and biological systems, learning can be an abrupt transition. A long approach, a sudden reorganization, a new regime that stays. In the brain, that reorganization can even be literally “switch-like” at the level of neural activity.

Now the caveat, because it is the line between an honest piece and a hyped one. The machine-learning papers make a formal claim: these jumps are phase transitions in the technical sense; critical points, order parameters, symmetry breaking. The neuroscience papers show something adjacent but not identical: that learning transitions are abrupt, and that the neural states switch rather than drift. They do not show that the brain sits at a critical point in the physicist’s sense. “Sudden” and “switch-like” are the phenomenology of a phase transition; they are not yet proof of one.

So the convergence is real, and tighter than a metaphor. Both are sudden reorganizations during learning, but still asymmetric. The formal machinery lives on the machine side. The brain gives us the phenomenon, the neural signature, and a hypothesis now concrete enough to test.

Where I’d push this

If learning really is a phase transition, the practical prize is obvious: a transition has a control parameter. Water doesn’t freeze on a whim. It freezes when you cross a line in temperature and pressure. If training has an equivalent, an order parameter that crosses a threshold when the capability appears, then knowing it means we could drive a network to that threshold on purpose. Reach the jump sooner. Stop paying for the long, flat plateau before grokking kicks in, which is where a huge share of the cost of modern AI is currently spent. Understanding the transition is not just satisfying. It could be a lever on training time.

And here is the idea I keep circling, and it runs straight back to Issue 1. There, the finding was that a single neuron is never one thing: it holds many attributes at once; many labels, superposed and mixed. A concept isn’t stored in a cell; it lives in how a whole population of these overlapping, multi-label units is combined.

If that’s true, learning a concept can’t be a matter of writing it down somewhere. It’s a matter of arrangement… Finding the one combination of many multi-attribute neurons that captures the structure at a higher level of abstraction. Not more units. A better configuration of the ones already there.

So here’s the bet. The phase transition of learning is that configuration clicking into place. For a long stretch the raw attributes are all present but badly arranged, which is exactly what a network looks like while it memorizes and fails to generalize. Then, at the critical point, the population settles into the encoding that is statistically optimal: the arrangement that optimizes some quantity; information, description length, free energy, that we haven’t yet named. Generalization doesn’t arrive because the network “understood.” It arrives because the distributed code crossed into its best configuration and stayed there.

That folds the two issues into a single claim. Issue 1: meaning is spread across many-attribute units. Issue 2: learning is the transition those units make into their optimal joint arrangement. One structure, seen twice… The distributed code, and the moment it snaps into the best version of itself.

I can’t prove it. It needs the order parameter in hand, the actual quantity being optimized, before it is more than a hunch. But that is the direction I’d dig.

Consider this one open-source: take it, run the math, collect your Nobel. I ask only that somewhere in the acceptance speech… Ideally right before you thank your parents 🤣 you nod to the guy who called it in a free newsletter and couldn’t prove a word of it. I’ll be in the back row, weeping with joy.

Sources

  • Wang, P. “Grokking as Dimensional Phase Transition in Neural Networks.” arXiv preprint (2026).

  • Le Pera, G., Nordio, C. “Learning as a Geometric Phase Transition…” arXiv preprint (2026).

  • Manzur, H. E., Vlasov, K., Jhong, Y.-J., Chen, H.-Y., Lin, S.-C. “The behavioral signature of stepwise learning strategy in male rats and its neural correlate in the basal forebrain.” Nature Communications 14, 4415 (2023).

  • Moore et al. “Revealing abrupt transitions from goal-directed to habitual behavior.” Nature Communications 17, 4751 (2026).

  • “Slow or sudden: re-interpreting the learning curve for modern systems neuroscience.” IBRO Neuroscience Reports (2022).

  • Gallistel, C. R., Fairhurst, S., Balsam, P. “The learning curve: implications of a quantitative analysis.” PNAS 101, 13124–13131 (2004).

Passionately Curious is written by Tugrul Guner — physics, biology, and AI, and the moments they turn out to be the same story. If this was worth your time, subscribe here and I’ll send the next one.

item.title: One Neuron, Many Meanings: Two 2026 Papers, One Result
item.description: A mouse cortex and artificial networks independently reach the same conclusion: meaning is carried by populations of neurons, not by single cells.
item.dc:creator: Tugrul Guner
item.content:encoded:
Two papers published in July 2026 arrive at the same conclusion from opposite ends of science. One, in Nature, maps the mouse cortex. The other, in Nature Machine Intelligence, is a mathematical framework for interpreting artificial neural networks. They share no authors and were not written in response to each other. Both find that the individual neuron, biological or artificial, is rarely a clean, single-purpose unit, and that what a network represents is distributed across populations of neurons rather than localized in any one cell.

Two independent results converging on the same structure is a stronger signal than either result alone. That is the reason to take this pair seriously.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The idea being tested

For much of the twentieth century, neuroscience operated under what is sometimes called the single-neuron doctrine: the assumption that individual cells encode specific, identifiable features; a neuron tuned to one face, the often-cited “grandmother cell.” The appeal was practical. If each neuron did one job, the brain could in principle be mapped one cell at a time.

The evidence below does not support that picture. It does not eliminate specialized neurons entirely, but it demotes them from the rule to the exception.

The brain: specialized neurons are the exception

The first paper, in Nature, is by Lorenzo Posani, Shuqi Wang, Stefano Fusi and colleagues: “Rarely categorical, highly separable representations along the cortical hierarchy.”

The team analyzed more than 14,000 neurons across 43 regions of the mouse cortex, using the International Brain Laboratory dataset, with all recordings taken during the same standardized behavioral task. That methodological detail resolves an old dispute. For decades, studies disagreed about whether the cortex organizes into distinct cell types, and much of the disagreement traced back to inconsistent methods including different tasks, different measurements. Here the same measurement was applied across the whole cortex.

The result is scale-dependent. Measured across the whole cortex, neural selectivity looks categorical and tracks anatomical organization. Measured within a single region, the categories largely disappear. Clean, specialized cell types were found reliably only in the primary sensory areas, the first stages of sensory processing. Elsewhere, neurons were diverse: each one responded to a combination of variables like color, shape, motion, reward value, rather than to a single feature. This property is called mixed selectivity.

Stefano Fusi, describing the specialized single-function neurons that earlier work had emphasized:

“We’re saying they are the exceptions. They’re not the rule.”

— Stefano Fusi

The diversity is not a measurement problem to be filtered out; it is functional. When each neuron combines variables in a slightly different way, the population represents information in a high-dimensional space. In that space, a wide range of possible classifications becomes linearly separable; a downstream region can decode them with a simple linear readout. High single-cell diversity is what makes the population flexible: one population can support many different computations, because no single neuron is committed to just one of them.

The machine: more concepts than neurons

The second paper, in Nature Machine Intelligence, is by David Klindt, Charles O’Neill, Nina Miolane and colleagues: “A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes.” It concerns artificial neural networks and contains no biology, but the parallel is direct.

A recurring obstacle in interpreting large models is that a given neuron often responds to several unrelated concepts at once. For example, legal language, French poetry, and the color teal. This is called polysemanticity, and it follows from a more fundamental property: superposition. A network can represent more distinct concepts than it has neurons by encoding each concept as a direction in activation space rather than as a dedicated unit. Those directions overlap and share the same physical neurons, which allows the network to store more features than a one-concept-per-neuron scheme would permit.

This is the artificial analogue of mixed selectivity. The two are not identical, and the distinction matters: mixed selectivity describes a single biological cell responding to a combination of task variables, while superposition is a specific claim about packing more features than neurons into a shared space by exploiting sparsity. They are different mechanisms. What they share is the consequence. The single unit is not the right level of description, and the representation lives in the geometry of the population.

The framework’s contribution is to explain when that representation can be recovered. It connects three previously separate results: identifiability theory, which shows that a trained network recovers its underlying features up to a linear mixing; compressed sensing, which gives conditions under which sparse, overlapping signals can be provably un-mixed; and interpretability metrics, which test whether recovered features correspond to human-recognizable concepts. Together they account for why methods such as sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from a superposed layer, and specify the conditions under which that extraction is guaranteed to work.

The shared result

In the brain, mixing many variables into each neuron makes the population high-dimensional and easy to read out. In artificial networks, mixing many concepts into each neuron lets a model store more than its neuron count would suggest while remaining recoverable by sparse methods. One team recorded mouse cortex; the other analyzed artificial networks. Neither was working toward the other’s result.

The common finding is that a distributed, high-dimensional code, not a set of labeled single units, is how both systems represent information. This is a candidate principle for how any distributed system encodes the world under pressure to be both efficient and flexible: represent each concept as a direction in a shared space rather than assigning one unit per concept. It holds across two very different substrates, which is what gives it weight.

What follows

For interpreting AI, the practical implication is specific. Searching a model for clean, human-labeled neurons looks for something the system does not contain; the more productive targets are the population’s geometry and the linear readouts that decode it, which is what the sparse-coding methods in the second paper are built to recover.

The obvious open question is whether the same organization holds in the human cortex. The Nature result is from mouse; work extending it to humans is underway. If it holds, the conclusion generalizes: across species and across substrates, the unit of representation is the population, and the single neuron is one component of it.
